items.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Rossano records and performs frequently on the Arbors label with bassist Nicki Parrott and drummer Eddie Metz.

ctx.x: Well said. When you say that you might try something that could be a challenge for the audience, are you talking about that term we sometimes use about playing “outside” the chord changes or being more experimental with the harmonies, comparing your right hand to your left hand?

Well I wouldn’t say much of that, because I am one of those players that is very much inside the harmony, even though I like very much almost everything in the history of jazz. But you see I specialized from Fats Waller to Teddy Wilson, and then the bebop, and then of course as a piano player I fell in love with the Bill Evans world. And that’s my thing is tonal jazz, so far. Then maybe one day I will feel the necessity to go in other directions. But for example, what I try always to explain to the audience is…

important, to be in the moment. You know, don’t go — in my opinion, I don’t want to go on stage with a preconceived set list that is going to happen, this and this and this. Because it takes away all the fun of it. The most beautiful feeling is when you get in front of the piano and the audience and you are blank. And you have to figure out what’s the right tune to play to make the people happy and yourself happy. And this was the approach that some of the greatest players used. I mean think of Errol Garner.…

items.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: So sometimes I might hire Rossano Sportiello over John DiMartino... I kind of have a pool of musicians I try to get

ctx.x: But you probably have people that you want to call in a certain order.

And sometimes for me it’s about the gig. Sometimes I think it might be a gig where they want it more traditional. So sometimes I might hire Rossano Sportiello over John DiMartino, do you know what I mean? It depends musically on what they want sometimes too. I kind of have a pool of musicians I try to get, basically.

Well you mentioned, amongst the things that you think about when you play, you think about sound. Is there a way that you can, as a bass player, how do you distinguish your own bass playing from any other thing.
